title: M*A*S*H: The Story of the 4077th
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the TV series M*A*S*H, its real-life origins, the 1968 novel by Richard Hornberger (Richard Hooker) and W.C. Heinz, Robert Altman's 1970 film, the show's production by Gene Reynolds and Larry Gelbart, its cast and character changes, notable episodes, the record-setting finale "Goodbye, Farewell and Amen," spinoffs, and a short listener mail item about a Howard Hughes photo misidentification.

segments.title: Tour promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming Canadian tour dates in Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto and how to get tickets.

segments.title: Opening banter on TV and MASH
segments.summary: Hosts discuss their differing feelings about MASH, Chuck's memories of watching it with his dad, Josh's childhood fandom, and the decline of half-hour sitcoms. Chuck explains the acronym and the three asterisks.

segments.title: Setting and real MASH units
segments.summary: The show is set in a mobile surgical hospital in the Korean War; real MASH units existed and had a high survival rate. Hosts discuss the Fox Ranch location in Malibu and how close units were to the front.

segments.title: Civilian drafted surgeons
segments.summary: The show's doctors were drafted civilians, younger and inexperienced, who resisted army culture, following the Doctors Draft Act after World War II and Korea. Alan Alda was 36 when the show started.

segments.title: Hornberger novel and its origins
segments.summary: The show and film were based on the 1968 novel MASH by Richard Hornberger (pen name Richard Hooker), co-written with W. C. Heinz, drawn from experiences of the 8055th unit. Hornberger was conservative, and Hollywood gave the material an anti-war slant. He later wrote fourteen MASH novels.

segments.title: Robert Altman's 1970 film
segments.summary: The 1970 film directed by Robert Altman was a hit, won the Palme d'Or, and earned five Oscar nominations including Best Screenplay. Ring Lardner Jr. disliked Altman's improvisational style; the hosts discuss the film's reception and Lardner's blacklisting.

segments.title: Theme song Suicide Is Painless
segments.summary: The movie's theme 'Suicide Is Painless' was written by Johnny Mandel and Altman's fifteen-year-old son Michael; the TV show used an instrumental version. Hosts digress on a film recommendation.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break in the episode for sponsor messages.

segments.title: Creation of the TV series
segments.summary: Altman disliked the TV version; Alan Alda was persuaded after reading the pilot. Producer Gene Reynolds and writer Larry Gelbart adapted the material, and the network compromised on laugh tracks, omitting them during surgery scenes.

segments.title: Laugh track and tone
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how the lack of a laugh track in dramatic scenes heightened the contrast, and compare it to other shows with laugh tracks removed or added.

segments.title: Run and ratings
segments.summary: MASH premiered September 1972 and ran to February 1983, initially opposite Wonderful World of Disney, then moved after All in the Family, becoming a top-rated show. Newsweek praised its morality.

segments.title: Main characters and cast
segments.summary: Hosts describe Hawkeye Pierce (Alan Alda), Trapper John (Wayne Rogers), BJ Hunnicutt (Mike Farrell), Radar O'Reilly (Gary Burghoff), Colonel Blake (McLean Stevenson), Colonel Potter (Harry Morgan), Frank Burns (Larry Linville), Charles Winchester (David Ogden Stiers), Hot Lips Houlihan (Loretta Swit), and Father Mulcahy (William Christopher), along with cast changes.

segments.title: Corporal Klinger and guest stars
segments.summary: Jamie Farr's Corporal Klinger began as a one-off character in women's clothing and became a regular. The hosts list notable one-episode guest stars such as Ron Howard, Leslie Nielsen, and Patrick Swayze.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break in the episode for sponsor messages.

segments.title: Special episodes
segments.summary: Hosts discuss very special MASH episodes: Sometimes You Hear a Bullet, Dreams, The Interview, Point of View, and the Season 3 finale Abyssinia, Henry, where Colonel Blake dies after leaving the show.

segments.title: Series finale Goodbye, Farewell and Amen
segments.summary: The two-and-a-half-hour finale was the most-watched TV episode in US history at that time, with about 121 million viewers and very expensive ad spots. Hosts discuss its ending montage and a plumbing urban legend. Chuck shares a family anecdote about watching it on videotape.

segments.title: Spinoffs and related shows
segments.summary: Hosts cover After M*A*S*H, Trapper John, M.D. (with Pernell Roberts), a dispute over The Pit and Crichton's ER, and the 1984 Walter pilot about Radar O'Reilly.

segments.title: Wrap-up on MASH
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the MASH discussion and suggest episodes to watch.

segments.title: Listener mail: Howard Hughes photo
segments.summary: Listener Martha Black pointed out that a photo of an older man identified as Howard Hughes in Vegas is actually actor Rip Torn, which the caption notes. Hosts also explain their email forwarding problems.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and direct listeners to contact the show.
